summary: Extends the RFC 1521 message format so that non-ASCII text can appear in email headers, such as in subject lines. It was designed to work with existing mail software. It was replaced by RFC 2045, RFC 2046, RFC 2047, RFC 2048, RFC 2049.

eli5.summary: Email headers once allowed only English letters. This memo gives a trick for writing other alphabets there without confusing old mail programs.

questions: how to put non-ascii text in email headers
what is the difference between q and b encoding
subtitle: How to put non-ASCII text, such as accented names, into email headers using encoded-words.

tldr.problem: Email headers were limited to ASCII, yet people need accented letters and other alphabets in names and subject lines, without upsetting existing mail software.
tldr.mechanism: Non-ASCII text is wrapped in an encoded-word of the form =?charset?encoding?encoded-text?=, using either the Q or the B encoding, in a few specific header locations.
tldr.outcome: Mail readers decode encoded-words for display, and old software sees only ordinary ASCII. RFC 1522 is obsoleted by RFC 2045 through RFC 2049.

today: RFC 1522 was a Draft Standard published in September 1993. It obsoletes RFC 1342 and is itself obsoleted by RFC 2045, RFC 2046, RFC 2047, RFC 2048 and RFC 2049.

sections.title: Non-ASCII Text in Mail Headers
sections.content:
RFC 1521 let message bodies use other character sets. RFC 1522 does the same for parts of the RFC 822 message header, in a way unlikely to confuse existing software. Some relaying programs delete some header fields, reorder addresses or header fields, or wrap headers at different places, and some readers choke on unusual RFC 822 features. So the memo avoids those features.

Instead it reserves ordinary printable ASCII sequences called encoded-words. A composer turns non-ASCII header text into encoded-words, and a reader that implements this memo reverses the encoding and shows the original text in the stated character set. Security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.eli5: It hides fancy letters inside ordinary ones, so old mail programs just pass them along while new ones can read them.

sections.title: The Encoded-Word Syntax
sections.content:
An encoded-word is =?charset?encoding?encoded-text?=. White space cannot appear between its parts. The charset can be any name allowed in an RFC 1521 text/plain charset parameter or registered with IANA for it, and ISO-8859-* sets are recommended when several would work. Charset and encoding names are case-independent.

An encoded-word may not be more than 75 characters long, and each header line containing one is limited to 76 characters. To encode more text, use several encoded-words separated by CRLF SPACE. The limits help gateways and limit how far a parser must look ahead for the closing ?=.
sections.eli5: An encoded-word is a small labeled box: it says which alphabet it uses, how it is packed, and what is inside. Boxes cannot be longer than 75 characters.

sections.title: The B and Q Encodings
sections.content:
Two encodings are defined. B is identical to the BASE64 encoding of RFC 1521. Q is similar to Quoted-Printable and keeps mostly-ASCII text readable. In Q, any 8-bit value can be written as = plus two hexadecimal digits (upper case), the underscore stands for a space (hex 20), and printable ASCII characters other than =, ?, _ and space may stand for themselves.

Q is recommended when most characters are ASCII, otherwise B should be used. A reader that handles encoded-words MUST accept either encoding for any character set it supports. Only printable and white space data should be encoded, and each encoded-word must hold whole octets and whole characters, so a multi-octet character cannot be split across adjacent encoded-words.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to pack the letters: one keeps English letters readable and only changes the odd ones, and the other scrambles everything into a safe code.

sections.title: Where Encoded-Words May Appear and How Readers Handle Them
sections.content:
An encoded-word may replace a text token in a Subject or Comments field, in extension and user-defined (X-) fields, inside a comment, or as a word in a phrase such as the name before an address in From, To or Cc. In a phrase, Q-encoded text is limited to letters, digits and a few punctuation characters. An encoded-word MUST NOT appear in an addr-spec or in a Received header field, and it must be separated from neighboring words by linear white space.

When displaying, a reader decodes encoded-words and ignores white space between two adjacent ones. If it does not support the charset it may show the raw text, make a best effort, or show a message. A badly formed encoded-word need not be displayed, but a reader MUST NOT refuse to display or handle the message because of it.
sections.eli5: Hidden letters are allowed in subject lines and in people's names, but never inside the actual address. If a box is broken, the reader should shrug and show the rest of the mail.
